Listen for a qualified decision and speaker positioning

**CORE-1: Learning goal and listening situation.** Follow a short discussion between an organizer and a venue/volunteer coordinator about taking an exhibition to other venues. Identify purpose, practical conditions, speaker stance and the final decision. B2; suggested 25–30 minutes. **Author/reviewer only: the assessed script below is NOT learner-facing before graded submit.**

**CORE-2: Teach the listening process.** On a first listen, identify the decision the group needs to make. On another focused listen, listen for shifts in position, reasons, contrast and conditions (*I would support that if…; that is not the same as…; before we commit…*). These phrases signal relationships, not fixed answers to look for. Take short notes if useful. **Separate written language example (not listening evidence):** In a meeting about a sports club's noticeboard, a volunteer says, “I like the idea, but only if we can display it indoors.” The speaker supports the idea conditionally rather than rejecting it. Do not use this example to guess the assessed dialogue. No mandatory number of replays, no transcript before graded submission, and no speed challenge as a proxy for proficiency.

**CORE-4: Feedback and repair (only after graded submission).** Offer the full transcript with aligned replay, contextual rationales and one optional short error repair: listen again for a contrast, a conditional phrase or the final action connected to the mistaken item. A fresh independent, written practice example: “We can reserve the room if the caretaker confirms the opening time.” Identify the action and requirement; this written exercise is **language preparation, not Listening evidence**. Never expose these exact assessed turns, feedback, source-bearing accessible labels or transcript elsewhere before graded submit. A failed/unavailable audio attempt is **UNASSESSED**, not a zero. All questions answered and verified full playback for this attempt are separate submit conditions. No oral production measurement.

**Media gate (hard):** Academic approval can validate script, item content, and anticipated CEFR difficulty, but not final spoken delivery. Until the original-rights MP3, measured duration/digest, script alignment, manifest, actual full-play/replay/retake guard, transcript concealment and browser/device QA pass, do not import this as an active evidence-weight-1 Listening lesson. Planned audio is not a completed asset or a score. If an independent reviewer requires acoustic or speaker-identification changes, fix script and review before generating audio.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of the discussion?

options.text: To design a permanent archive tour covering every hall
To compare the archive's ticket prices with other venues
To plan a limited trial and establish conditions for proceeding and evaluating it
To decide which archive objects should be sold

items.rationale: Mara sets the planning purpose and limited funding; the final decision is a conditional two-venue trial.
items.misconception: interpreting a request from three halls as an accepted commitment.
items.repair: on post-submit replay, listen to the opening purpose and final statement together.

items.prompt: What does Jon identify as a reason to consider the East Hall despite its smaller size?

options.text: Its visitors may include people who seldom travel to the main archive.
It has promised a larger craft-group audience than North Hall.
It provides free transport for the original glass cases.
It opens every morning and evening throughout the trial.

items.rationale: Jon says some East Hall people rarely travel to the main archive; reaching them could matter more than crowd size.
items.misconception: treating capacity as the sole selection criterion.
items.repair: listen for the contrast after “much smaller” and the intended audience.

items.prompt: What is Jon's position on the practical feasibility of visiting both halls?

options.text: She prefers to display original objects regardless of staffing.
She refuses both visits because volunteers are unavailable.
She will support both only if the visits take place on Saturdays.
She supports both conditionally, as long as lighter printed displays replace the difficult-to-move original objects.

items.rationale: She can staff one Saturday and one Tuesday and explicitly conditions support on lightweight panels with printed copies.
items.misconception: hearing a logistical objection as complete rejection.
items.repair: replay the sentence starting “I'd support both halls if…”, after submission.

items.prompt: What information would Mara's proposed optional question collect?

options.text: Whether visitors want to become paid archive members
Whether visitors have visited the archive before
Whether visitors would rather use glass cases or panels
How many minutes visitors can stay at each venue

items.rationale: Mara proposes a voluntary, anonymous first-visit question to complement attendance.
items.misconception: confusing evaluation of reach with evaluation of every aspect of the experience.
items.repair: contrast the question's actual focus with the broader trial goals.

items.prompt: Suppose the North trial later records 80 attendees and the East trial records 35, but the voluntary feedback has not yet been examined. Which conclusion would be consistent with the speakers' evaluation plan?

options.text: North was more effective at reaching people unfamiliar with the archive.
East was necessarily more successful because its venue was smaller.
North recorded higher attendance, but relative success in reaching new visitors is not yet established.
Both events reached the same number of new visitors because both used printed copies.

items.rationale: The hypothetical figures show different attendance totals; Jon cautions against treating raw counts as success, and Mara proposes separate information about prior visits. None of the other options follows from the stated plan.
items.misconception: interpreting a larger total as necessarily greater success.
items.repair: distinguish the observed count from the intended audience outcome and identify what more information the team needs.

items.prompt: What is authorized by the final decision?

options.text: Booking all three halls immediately, then checking safety later
Preparing a plan for North and East and booking only after panel safety and venue agreement are confirmed
Replacing the main archive with a permanent travelling display
Booking the North Hall alone and dropping the evaluation

items.rationale: Mara's final statement records preparation, checks and conditional booking, not a permanent tour.
items.repair: replay the final sentence and list the action and its prerequisites separately.

proposed_manifest.source:
A: The Fern Bridge archive has been asked to take a small display to three neighbourhood halls. We have enough transport funding for two visits this term. Before choosing venues, we need to decide what a useful first trial would look like, not promise every hall a visit.
B: The North Hall offered us Saturday mornings and expects a fairly large audience because its craft group meets then. The East Hall suggested a Tuesday afternoon. It is much smaller, but the manager says some people there rarely travel to the main archive. If the point is to reach people who do not already visit us, a large crowd is not the only thing to consider.
A: Can the volunteers manage that combination with our existing display?
B: I can provide a team on one Saturday and one Tuesday, but the boxes need to be lighter. Our previous display used glass cases, and moving those safely would take more people than we have. I'd support both halls if we use printed copies on lightweight panels rather than original objects.
A: That makes sense. We also need a sensible way of evaluating the visits. The managers could tell us attendance, but those numbers alone wouldn't reveal whether we reached new visitors. Could we ask one optional, anonymous question about whether someone has visited the archive before?
B: Yes, provided we make it clear that people can enjoy the display without answering. We should not compare raw attendance and call the larger event more successful. The venues have different opening hours and capacities.
A: Let's also confirm that both venues can accommodate the lightweight panels before we book transport.
B: Yes. That gives us a realistic plan to take back to the venue managers.
A: Agreed. We will prepare a two-venue trial plan for North and East, check panel safety and venue agreement, then book only if those checks pass. We'll review attendance, voluntary first-visit feedback and the team's workload afterwards. We haven't made a permanent tour commitment.

1. LIS-B2-02 — Follow the structure of an extended explanation
**CORE-1 — Goal and context.** You are helping a school club understand a talk about a trial for improving a shared space. After listening, identify the purpose, how supporting points are organised, a limitation and the next step. Focus on meaning rather than catching every word.

**CORE-2 — Learn the method.** On the first listen, identify the speaker's main question and rough stages (context → proposal → support → limitation → next step). On a focused listen, attach details to the stage they support. Signals like “however”, “for instance”, “the point is”, and “before we decide” can reveal structure, but do not treat them as automatic answer keys. A claim that something *may* help is not proof that it did. Separate what was observed from what is only proposed.

**Independent worked demonstration (reading about listening strategy, not assessed audio):** “The garden club wants to reuse pots. One volunteer has sorted the clean ones. However, the shed has no dry shelf. Before buying more pots, the club will check whether existing shelves can be rearranged.” Main goal: find a feasible reuse arrangement. Sorting is a supporting preparation detail; the dry shelf is a limitation; checking storage is the next step, not a purchase. A tempting wrong note is “Buy more pots” because it ignores “before”. This miniature model uses different facts from the assessed script. 
Learner-facing pre-playback situation only: A volunteer explains a possible improvement to a school club's shared space. First listen for the purpose. Then listen again for evidence, limitations and the proposed next step. Do not reveal the following transcript or answers until the assessment is submitted.

**Independent objective items (reviewer key and rationales; render explanations only post-submit).**

LIS-B2-02-Q1 — listening.gist. What is the overall purpose of the talk?
- A. Announce a permanent expansion of the school hall. — Wrong setting and decision status.
- B. Explain observations and propose a cautious improvement trial for the quiet room. — **Key B.** Connects the initial purpose, observations, space concern and limited next action.
- C. Compare students' reading scores before and after lunch. — No learning scores are mentioned.
- D. Prove that students no longer need the quiet room. — The speaker aims to improve it, not discontinue it.

LIS-B2-02-Q2 — listening.detail. Why did some newcomers stand at the door?
- A. They were unsure whether permission was required. — **Key A.** The volunteer's observation explicitly concerns entry arrangements.
- B. The door was locked during lunch. — No lock is reported.
- C. They were waiting for an exam. — No exam is mentioned.
- D. They had been told all seats were taken. — This invents an explanation.

LIS-B2-02-Q3 — listening.detail. What is the speaker's concern about adding chairs?
- A. They would cost more than a sign. — No price comparison is made.
- B. They would prevent students from reading. — Unsupported absolute consequence.
- C. They might obstruct movement through the room. — **Key C.** The narrow route is the stated concern.
- D. The caretaker had already refused to move furniture. — A safety check is proposed, not a refusal.

LIS-B2-02-Q4 — listening.inference. Which note accurately preserves the status of the sign?
- A. “Sign already approved; permanent.” — Conflicts with explicit lack of approval.
- B. “Sign shown to improve grades.” — No such evidence.
- C. “Sign unnecessary because everyone understands.” — Contradicts the observation.
- D. “Temporary trial possible, subject to school agreement; effect not known.” — **Key D.** Preserves conditional status and uncertain effect.

LIS-B2-02-Q5 — listening.detail. What does the speaker recommend checking before the trial?
- A. Whether the caretaker considers the proposed layout safe. — **Key A.** The speaker explicitly proposes asking the caretaker first.
- B. Whether another school has purchased chairs. — Not part of the plan.
- C. Whether students have paid for the shelves. — Unsupported.
- D. Whether a volunteer can teach a reading class. — Not the stated next action.

LIS-B2-02-Q6 — listening.inference. If newcomers still ask how to enter during the trial, what conclusion is consistent with the talk?
- A. The quiet room must be closed. — Unsupported drastic response.
- B. The sign may not be enough; consider explaining the arrangements differently. — **Key B.** Follows the speaker's proposed decision criterion without claiming causation.
- C. The furniture definitely caused the confusion. — The talk does not establish this causal connection.
- D. All students dislike the room. — The observation cannot justify that conclusion.

**CORE-4 — Repair and next action.** Q1/Q4/Q6: revisit the speaker's overall intention and mark uncertain vs decided. Q2/Q3/Q5: replay the relevant sections after submission and attach each detail to its supporting point. A wrong answer is a cue to revisit the relevant segment, not a CEFR diagnosis.

Make a blank five-part listening-note frame (purpose, observation, proposed action, limitation, next step) and explain how you would record uncertainty; do not invent facts or a listening score. A future separate real audio is required for actual transfer evidence.

proposed_manifest.source:
Last month, our school opened a small quiet room where students could spend part of the lunch break. The original idea was to offer an alternative to the crowded hall, especially for students who wanted to read or finish a small piece of work. We are now considering how to make the room more useful, rather than simply increasing the number of chairs.

Let me explain what we noticed during the first two weeks. Several students used the room regularly, but the volunteer on duty said that newcomers sometimes stood at the door because they were unsure whether they needed permission to enter. That is an observation about how the room was used, not evidence that students disliked it. A clearer sign could help newcomers understand the basic arrangements.

There is also a practical issue with space. The room has a narrow route between the shelves and the tables. Adding more chairs might make it harder for people to move around. Instead, we could try moving one table nearer the window, while keeping the route clear. The caretaker would need to check that the arrangement is safe.

I should emphasise that neither suggestion has been approved yet. We also do not know whether a sign alone would change how students use the room. Before deciding, I would suggest asking the caretaker about the layout, then trying a temporary sign for a week if the school agrees. Volunteers could note whether newcomers still ask how to enter. That information would help us decide whether the sign should stay, or whether we need to explain the arrangements in another way.

2. LIS-B2-03 — Select notes that preserve evidence and limitations
**CORE-1 — Goal and context.** You are preparing notes for a library meeting after a report on a book-exchange trial. Distinguish a reported observation, an example, a limitation, and a conditional recommendation. Select useful details without transcribing every sentence.

**CORE-2 — Learn the method.** Use a compact note structure: claim/question | observed support | exception/limit | next action. Separate numbers from their denominators or context; a count of responses is not the whole population. When the speaker says “some”, “among those who replied”, “we cannot yet tell”, or gives an example, preserve the scope. Do not convert reported comments into measured outcomes. A good note is short but not less accurate than the original.

**Independent worked demonstration (different content):** “Eight people replied to a survey about an after-school drawing session. Six of those eight liked the time. We have not heard from students who could not attend. Ask them before changing the schedule.” Notes: six of eight respondents liked time; non-attendees absent; consult them before change. “Most students approve” wrongly changes the denominator and generalises beyond respondents. The example teaches the method, not the assessed facts.
Learner-facing pre-playback situation: A library coordinator reports on a trial. On the first listen identify the question being investigated; on subsequent listens choose notes that preserve the evidence and limits. Transcript reviewer/production-only until submitted.

proposed_manifest.source:
We have finished the first month of a small book-exchange trial at the community library. The exchange is designed for people who want to pass on a book they have read and choose another one, without needing to buy anything. We wanted to find out whether the arrangement was easy to use, not whether it increased the amount of reading in the whole neighbourhood.

We collected two kinds of information. First, the volunteers kept a record of books placed on the exchange shelf. They recorded forty-six additions over four Saturdays. That number tells us how often books were added. It does not tell us how many different people contributed, because the same person could bring several books. Secondly, we invited visitors to leave a short comment. Fourteen of the eighteen people who chose to comment said the instructions were clear. Two comments mentioned that the shelf was difficult to reach when the nearby reading table was busy.

We must be careful about treating those comments as representative. Some visitors did not leave a comment, and we did not ask people who had never tried the exchange. In other words, the feedback can help us improve the shelf, but it cannot tell us what everyone in the neighbourhood thinks. One volunteer suggested opening another exchange point at the sports centre. That might be worth considering later, although nobody has checked whether the sports centre has suitable space or staff.

For the next month, I would recommend keeping the existing shelf and testing a different position for the reading table, subject to the library manager's agreement. We can ask both users and non-users about accessibility. After that, we can decide whether an additional exchange point is justified. We should not announce an expansion before we understand the practical requirements.

3. LIS-B2-04 — Track speaker positions, qualifications and decisions
**CORE-1 — Goal and context.** You are helping a community committee prepare a neutral account of a discussion about a possible repair workshop. Follow two speakers' changing positions, distinguish agreement on a limited step from agreement on a full plan, and infer the evidence that matters to each speaker.

**CORE-2 — Learn the method.** Draw a two-column note grid, one column per speaker. For each, capture initial view, reason, concern, response to new information and final position. “I could support it if…” is conditional, not full agreement; “I see your point” acknowledges another view without necessarily adopting it. Listen for references and qualification across turns, not isolated keywords. A final plan may be narrower than the initial suggestion.

**Independent worked demonstration (different content):** “Nora: I'd like a weekly music club. Ken: I support music activities, but we don't know if a room is free every week. Nora: Then could we check for a single trial session first? Ken: Yes, let's ask about one session.” Notes: Nora shifts from weekly plan to a trial enquiry; Ken supports asking about availability, not weekly sessions. Agreement is on an enquiry only. Do not infer Ken dislikes music. 
Learner-facing pre-playback situation: Two committee members discuss an activity proposal. Listen for initial positions, reasons and the final decision. The following script is reviewer/recording-only until submission.

Lina: I've been thinking about the unused corner of the community hall. Several neighbours have asked where they can get help with simple repairs, such as tightening a loose screw or replacing a missing button. I wondered whether we could run a monthly repair workshop. People might learn a useful skill as well as keeping an item for longer.

Ben: I like the educational purpose, but I'm not ready to promise a monthly event. Last time the hall hosted a practical activity, the organisers needed someone who could supervise the equipment and make sure the space was left clear. We haven't established who would take responsibility for that.

Lina: That's fair. I hadn't thought about the supervision arrangements. I wasn't imagining electrical repairs or anything involving dangerous equipment. We could start with ordinary clothes repairs and simple demonstrations using safe materials.

Ben: That narrows the proposal, which makes it easier to discuss. Even so, I'd want to know whether there are volunteers with the appropriate skills and whether the hall manager is comfortable with the plan. We should also find out what residents actually want to learn rather than assume that the requests we've heard reflect everyone.

Lina: Instead of asking the manager to approve a regular programme now, how about asking whether a single supervised demonstration would be possible? We could invite residents to suggest topics on a short voluntary form before planning the session.

Ben: I could support that enquiry. If the manager agrees in principle, we can then check volunteer availability and the suitable materials. But we shouldn't advertise a date or invite people to bring items yet.

Lina: Agreed. I'll draft a short message asking the manager about a possible demonstration. You can help me make sure it doesn't promise anything.

Ben: Yes. The decision today is to ask, not to run the workshop. We can discuss whether a longer programme is worthwhile once we know more.

1. LIS-C1-01 — Trace a lecturer's argument beyond explicit signposts
**CORE-1 — Goal/context.** Follow a short extended lecture in which the speaker first presents an apparently attractive interpretation, then revises its scope. Distinguish the main proposition, illustrative counterexample, qualification and methodological implication. Make concise notes without turning a rhetorical setup into the lecturer's conclusion.
**CORE-2 — Learn the method.** Note what each segment *does*, not every word: introduces a tempting view; provides an example; exposes an assumption; qualifies; draws a limited implication. An example may be a counterexample rather than supporting evidence. Expressions such as “the difficulty with that account”, “what follows is not that…”, or “the distinction matters because…” can signal a change in argumentative function; meaning across sentences, not the marker alone, decides. Distinguish a lecturer's reported view from the view endorsed.
Independent written model (not assessed source): “A theatre's booking page lists every performance. It is tempting to call that equal access. Yet the page cannot tell us whether a visitor can reach the building. This does not make the page useless; it makes the claim about access too broad.” Note: listing coverage ≠ practical access; counterexample is travel; value retained; narrower claim. Common error: “The speaker opposes the booking page.” The speaker rejects the broad claim, not the tool. 
Learner-facing situation before audio: A lecturer discusses how a digital catalogue can shape interpretation of a collection. First listen for the line of argument; then note the role of examples and the limits of the conclusion. Do not expose the assessed transcript or answers.

- B. Modern terminology should be excluded from archive searches. — Speaker accepts its benefits.

- D. Archive research is reliable only when original materials are difficult to locate. — Speaker explicitly rejects preserving all difficulty.

proposed_manifest.source:
When an archive makes its catalogue searchable, we tend to imagine that a previously inaccessible collection has simply become visible. That is a reasonable starting point, provided we remember what is meant by visibility. A catalogue can make a document much easier to locate; it can also determine which document is likely to be located in the first place. Those are related benefits and risks, rather than two separate technologies.

Consider a fictional collection of notebooks from an amateur weather society. Some contributors recorded observations under the names of villages, while others used informal descriptions such as the fields beyond the railway. A search organised around current place names would make the first group of notebooks relatively easy to retrieve. The second group would not necessarily be missing from the collection, nor would it necessarily be less valuable. It would be less likely to appear in the results of that particular search. The distinction matters because a researcher could mistake an uneven route into the collection for an uneven distribution of historical observations.

One might respond that a more comprehensive set of labels would solve the problem. It would certainly help. But there is a complication: a label that makes sense to a present-day reader may not faithfully represent the categories used by the people who produced the records. If we replace every ambiguous description with a confident modern equivalent, we may be making a decision on the researcher's behalf while appearing merely to improve the interface. That is not an argument for preserving every difficulty of the original material. It is an argument for making consequential editorial choices visible.

Notice that the example does not establish how often such a distortion occurs in actual archives. It describes a mechanism by which it could occur. Measuring its prevalence would require a different investigation. For our purposes, the immediate question is whether a catalogue allows a reader to distinguish what was originally written, what an editor has inferred, and what has been left uncertain. A useful catalogue need not answer every historical question. It should make it possible to recognise which questions the catalogue itself cannot answer.

2. LIS-C1-02 — Infer the logic of challenges and concessions in a debate
**CORE-1 — Goal/context.** Follow a two-speaker debate on how to assess a programme. Reconstruct each speaker's underlying criterion, detect when a challenge concerns interpretation rather than the data, and identify a concession that narrows rather than abandons a position.

A supports repeating it because it attracted attention; B accepts the count but asks whether the aim was attention or acquiring a skill. Asha: Our mentoring programme was meant to make the transition into the school less intimidating. The pilot attracted more applications than places, and most participants completed all four meetings. I would hesitate to redesign something before giving it a fair chance to develop. We have at least established that students were willing to take part.

Daniel: I don't dispute that. What troubles me is the language in the draft report: it says the pilot improved students' confidence. Completing four meetings is compatible with feeling more confident, but also with feeling obliged to attend once a teacher has introduced you to a mentor. The problem isn't the attendance figure; it's the job we are asking that figure to do.

Asha: Fair enough. The report should say participation was sustained rather than confidence improved. But I wouldn't treat the absence of confidence measures as a reason to suspend the meetings. If we insist on collecting perfect evidence before any activity can continue, the students who might benefit would lose the opportunity while we design our evaluation.

Daniel: I'm not asking for perfect evidence. I am asking whether the programme might be evaluated in a way that gives the students who did not apply some visibility. If the participants were already comfortable asking for help, high attendance might tell us very little about reaching those who find the school hardest to navigate. A short confidential invitation to a wider group could explore that question without requiring them to identify themselves to the mentors.

Asha: That changes how I'd frame the next stage. I'd still keep a small version of the existing programme available, but I would not describe it as a successful intervention yet. The wider invitation could inform whether the next version needs a different entry route. We should be clear that a response to the invitation would be evidence of a reported experience, not a direct measure of changed confidence.

Daniel: I could accept that distinction. My remaining reservation is that we should set a review point before expanding the number of places. Otherwise an initially modest continuation can become a permanent commitment without anyone explicitly deciding it. If the report records the continuation as provisional, and states what is still unknown, I wouldn't oppose it.

Asha: Then we agree on maintaining access at a limited scale while reconsidering the way we evaluate it. The decision about expansion remains open. Neither of us has evidence yet that mentoring caused an improvement in confidence.

3. LIS-C1-03 — Interpret implied positioning and reconstruct a qualified conclusion
**CORE-1 — Goal/context.** In an interview, identify a speaker's indirect resistance to a question's premise, distinguish a pragmatic qualification from a denial, and reconstruct the position without attributing an exaggerated claim. Use a note grid for attributed claims, implied limits, evidential status and decisions.
**CORE-2 — Learn the method.** An interviewer may frame an issue as a forced choice; a speaker can reject the framing rather than choose one side. Expressions such as “that is one way to describe it”, “I would put it differently”, or a question in return may politely challenge a premise. Infer the function using the full turn and subsequent clarification; tone alone is insufficient. Do not infer private motives. A qualified answer can acknowledge both a benefit and a cost, with a narrower recommendation.
Independent written example: Interviewer: “So the evening class failed?” Tutor: “That depends on what it was expected to achieve. It gave existing learners extra practice; it did not attract many new learners. I'd revise the invitation rather than describe the class as unsuccessful.” Note: rejects single success/failure frame; different goals, different outcomes; retains activity with revision.

Host: You've moved part of the feedback process from written comments to brief consultations. The trial report says students asked fewer follow-up questions afterwards. Is that an indication that the consultations are simply more effective than written feedback?

Organiser: It is one possible interpretation, although I'd put the comparison slightly differently. A written comment remains available when a student returns to a draft two days later; a conversation can allow the student to question a suggestion immediately. We were trying to understand when each form of feedback is useful. Counting later questions gives us a small part of that picture.

Host: But surely fewer questions means there was less confusion. Otherwise why would you have introduced the consultations in the first place?

Organiser: Fewer recorded questions means exactly that. A student may have resolved a difficulty during a consultation, but another may have decided not to raise a further question. We did not collect the same information about both students' reasons. I would rather not let the convenience of a count make that count a substitute for the thing we want to understand.

Host: So are you suggesting the trial hasn't told you very much?

Organiser: Not about a general improvement in understanding, no. It has told us something more specific. Several students who attended said that discussing one unclear comment helped them decide what to do next. Other students said they wanted to retain a written record so they could revisit the advice. Those reports are useful for planning a subsequent version, even though they do not tell us how many students improved their work as a result.

Host: If both forms have a purpose, the obvious answer would be to offer every student a full consultation and a full set of written comments.

Organiser: That might be desirable in an ideal timetable. The issue in this particular department is how to use the same allocation of staff time. We could test written comments with a brief optional clarification slot, especially for students who cannot identify a next step. I wouldn't promise identical access to individual consultations until we know what scheduling is feasible.

Host: Then your position is that a consultation is a supplement rather than a replacement?

Organiser: For the next limited trial, yes. I would not turn that into a general rule for every subject or every student. The aim is to see whether students can explain and carry out a next revision step, and to collect feedback from those who do not request a consultation. If we learn that the arrangement leaves some students with unresolved difficulties, that would be a reason to reconsider it.

Mira: The exhibition includes short extracts from interviews with former residents. I'd like to organise the extracts around common themes rather than present each interview in its entirety. Visitors who have only ten minutes might otherwise struggle to make sense of the collection. The difficulty is deciding whether our arrangement helps visitors encounter the accounts or effectively tells them what those accounts mean.

Leon: That's the distinction I wanted to raise. If we place two extracts under a label such as “nostalgia”, the label might lead visitors to interpret both accounts in the same way, even if one speaker was expressing a reservation about the past. I wouldn't oppose thematic organisation in principle. I would want the original context to remain accessible and the label to be recognisable as our editorial choice.

Mira: I can see why that matters. The observation from the small preview was that visitors moved through the themed section more quickly. That might mean the organisation made navigation easier, but we did not ask whether they understood the speakers' different positions. It would be misleading to claim that faster movement meant deeper understanding. Perhaps the extracts could be presented under questions rather than interpretive labels.

Leon: Questions could reduce the risk, although even a question can imply a particular way of reading an account. I would favour giving visitors a way to return to a longer segment, with a brief explanation of why the extract was selected. We should make sure the speakers' consent covers that presentation, rather than assuming permission for one format automatically covers another.

Mira: Then let's prepare a small example of the question-led arrangement, subject to the agreed permissions, and invite a few visitors to explain how they interpreted the different extracts. We can compare that with a version that follows the interview order. I would not describe either arrangement as better before we have investigated the actual differences.

Leon: That sounds like a worthwhile comparison. My support is for preparing and evaluating the examples, not committing the whole exhibition to a particular structure. If the comparison reveals that a concise arrangement loses an important qualification, we will need to revise the arrangement even if visitors move through it more quickly.

A: When we met last month, I argued that the shared directory was reducing the amount of time volunteers spent answering routine questions. I had based that view partly on the enquiry log: it showed fewer requests to the central desk during the trial. I also had the impression that volunteers at the smaller centres were finding the directory useful. I still think the idea deserves attention, but the way I described the evidence needs revisiting.

B: The change in requests to the central desk is real, as far as the log goes. The difficulty is that the smaller centres started keeping their own enquiry records halfway through the trial. Before that, a request referred to the central desk was much more likely to appear in the central log. We don't have a consistent network-wide count for the two periods. So it is possible that work shifted between desks without the overall amount of work falling.

A: That is an important distinction. I had treated the central desk as if it were the whole network. The figures could still tell us something about where requests were handled, but they cannot settle whether volunteers saved time. I wouldn't want to lose the observation about the central desk altogether. We need to narrow the claim, rather than pretend the log tells us nothing.

B: And there is a second issue. Some volunteers reported that they could find the standard forms more quickly. Others said they spent longer checking whether the version they had found was current. Those were comments from an optional discussion, not timed observations of everyone using the system. We can use them to identify two different things to investigate: retrieval and verification. It would be misleading to average impressions and call the result a time saving.

A: In that case I would change the request I brought to this meeting. Instead of asking the committee to roll the directory out to every centre, I would ask whether we can design a comparison in which participating centres use the same enquiry categories and record time spent both finding and checking a document. We should also keep the existing route for people who cannot use the directory. There may be a benefit even if the total number of enquiries does not change, but that is a question for the evaluation, not a result we already have.

B: I can support developing that plan. We have not yet agreed how many centres can take part or who would check the consistency of the records. Let's agree that we will draft the measurement plan and ask the centre coordinators what capacity they have. We are not authorising another trial today, let alone a network-wide rollout. If we return with a feasible proposal, the committee can make a separate decision.

When people visit a restored building, they are often invited to notice the parts that have been returned to their original condition. There is a reassuring simplicity to that invitation, although the word original conceals a choice. Buildings have histories rather than a single birthday. One visitor may have in mind the day the building opened, another the period in which it became familiar to the neighbourhood. A later alteration can be historically significant without having been part of the first design. Let me use an imaginary restoration to illustrate why the way we explain such choices matters.

The exhibition team has prepared two diagrams of a small assembly hall. The first depicts the hall at the time of its opening; the second identifies additions made during the years in which it served as a training centre. A member of the team objects: if we show visitors both diagrams, surely we will undermine the claim that the restoration is historically faithful. I think the objection deserves a better answer than simply insisting that more information is always beneficial. Two diagrams could indeed create confusion if neither made clear which period it depicted. But the uncertainty in that case would be a feature of the explanation, not an inevitable consequence of showing more than one period.

There is another argument that sounds rather attractive. We might say that the building should be allowed to speak for itself. I would welcome that principle if it meant not dictating what visitors ought to feel. If, however, it meant presenting the restored hall without indicating which surviving features were retained and which were reconstructed, the apparent neutrality of the display would depend on visitors overlooking decisions that had already been made on their behalf. The absence of an explanatory label would not remove the interpretation; it would make its origin harder to identify.

This is where we need to distinguish uncertainty about a historical fact from openness about its significance. The team may be able to establish when a partition was installed and still have good reason to leave open the question of which period is most meaningful to a visitor. Conversely, inviting different personal responses is no substitute for acknowledging that a particular construction date is uncertain. In neither case do we improve the exhibition by pretending the other kind of uncertainty has disappeared.

My recommendation is therefore not to turn every label into a history of the entire building. Identify the period and evidence relevant to the restoration decision, mark any uncertainty in that evidence, and indicate how a visitor can examine the other period if it interests them. We can explain why a choice was made without suggesting that it is the only legitimate way to value the building. That, rather than the production of an apparently definitive account, is the kind of historical fidelity I would defend.

Moderator: The storytelling programme has been running in small neighbourhood groups. A proposal would bring some sessions together in a larger hall. Before we talk about a trial, I'd like to know what each of you would count as continuity. The word appears in all three of your notes, but I suspect you mean rather different things by it.

Leena: From the point of view of the coordinators, continuity means that a group can still meet when its usual facilitator is away. At present, when a session is cancelled, the other groups can't readily offer a replacement because their rooms are small. The larger hall might allow a session to go ahead with a substitute. I'm not saying people would necessarily attend it. We haven't tried the arrangement.

Tomas: For me the continuity worth protecting is the conversation itself. In the smaller group, someone can refer to a story told three weeks ago and expect the others to know what they mean. Bringing groups together might create new connections, which I welcome, but a larger meeting could also interrupt that shared thread. A record showing that the scheduled session took place would not tell us whether that continuity was preserved.

Ruth: And I would distinguish both from continuity of access. A participant might know the group and be willing to talk, but not be able to reach the larger hall. The travel enquiry we ran asked people already attending sessions how they usually got there. It did not ask those who had stopped attending. I don't want an apparently reassuring set of replies to settle a question we didn't ask.

Moderator: Leena, would you accept Tomas's point that a session can go ahead and still lose something the programme values?

Leena: Entirely. I would still like to know whether we can avoid cancellations, but I wouldn't call the number of meetings an adequate success measure. In fact, I'd prefer to test a substitute arrangement in one existing group before assuming that bringing groups together is the way to achieve it.

Tomas: That would make the question more manageable. I would not make a new facilitator reproduce every earlier conversation. I'd ask whether participants can pick up a topic they consider important and whether newcomers can join it. Those are two different possibilities, and continuity need not mean that nothing changes.

Ruth: I could support investigating that smaller option, provided the enquiry includes people who haven't been coming recently. I don't yet have evidence about why they stopped. I wouldn't want the plan to assume it was travel, or assume it wasn't.

Moderator: So there are at least three things to design for: whether a session can be maintained, whether conversations can develop, and who can actually take part. Can we agree to draft an evaluation plan for one existing group, including a way to invite views from non-attenders, and establish whether a substitute is available? A trial itself would need a separate decision.

Leena: Yes, that's a useful first step.

Tomas: Yes, provided the conversation measures aren't reduced to attendance.

Ruth: And provided the enquiry doesn't presume the reason someone stopped attending.

Chair: The former quarry is being considered for a short public interpretation trail. Some correspondence makes it sound as though we have to decide between preserving a working landscape and providing access. I wonder whether that is quite the decision before us. We're discussing a trial route, not the eventual management of the whole site.

Ecologist: That distinction helps, but I would not want the temporary route to become the default simply because it has been used. A survey last spring identified a sheltered section where nesting activity was recorded. It didn't establish that every part of the quarry is equally sensitive. Nor did it establish that the sheltered section will remain occupied throughout the year. My concern is with what would count as a reason to change a route once visitors have become accustomed to it.

Historian: I have heard the suggestion that we should put the interpretation panels at the points with the best surviving industrial features. That sounds reasonable, until you realise that some of the most informative traces are also the least visible from the permitted path. I am not asking for access to every trace. I would rather that the interpretation acknowledged the limits of what can be seen, instead of treating the visible features as a representative sample.

Chair: So, could we agree that a route might be useful even if it is not representative of the entire site?

Historian: Certainly, provided the panels explain the distinction. I would not call it an account of the whole quarry.

Ecologist: I can accept that description. What I cannot accept is an assumption that an educational route is therefore environmentally acceptable. If we trial it, the stopping condition needs to be explicit. I would support a reversible route outside the sheltered section, subject to a current survey.

Chair: That sounds like support for a trial with conditions, rather than agreement that this is the right permanent route. May I record it that way?

Ecologist: Yes. And if the survey calls the route into question, the trial should not start. If conditions change later, it should be suspended.

Historian: From my side, I would add that the panels should not imply that everything absent from the route is unimportant. A visitor should understand why a partial account is being offered.

Chair: Then the shared proposal is to prepare a reversible route and a qualified interpretation plan, pending the survey and the site committee's approval. We have not decided a permanent route, and we have not settled how future access should be balanced against conservation. I will record those as separate unresolved matters.

CORE-1: Produce a nuanced report for a fictional archive steering group, synthesising a policy note, a participant letter and a fresh recorded interview. Distinguish interpretive value, representativeness, permission and practical scope; revise a claim and report structure when a counter-reading is defensible.
CORE-2: Topic: neighbourhood sound archive; Task: decision-oriented report, not promotional copy; Must Include: attributed evidence from each mode, a fair opposing position, bounded proposal, unresolved questions, substantive revision log; Boundary: no invented consent, causal effect, representative coverage or approval. Brainstorm source claims and their limits; group by decision questions rather than by source. Outline supported finding → competing criteria → conditional recommendation → next evidence needed. 
Independent worked model on a fictional recipe manuscript exhibit: a curator reports all donated manuscripts were catalogued, a residents' note says many recipes were never donated, a trustee offers a temporary display subject to permissions. Weak thesis: “The collection represents the town and is ready for display.” Revised thesis: “Cataloguing is complete for the donated manuscripts; the collection cannot establish town-wide practice, and a temporary display remains conditional on permissions.” The revised claim preserves achievement but distinguishes scope and decision. Organise the brief by what is known, what is missing and what can be authorised, not by three source summaries. A revision that only replaces “ready” with “prepared” does not repair the inference. 
CORE-3 — fresh independent sources (distinct from both scored lessons).
Written source A, project note: The archive has indexed every recording received during a six-week invitation. Contributors were asked to record an everyday sound and explain its significance; the invitation was circulated through three neighbourhood groups. People could choose whether to contribute. Indexing is complete, but the project has no register of all potential contributors or of sounds that were not submitted. Staff propose a small listening exhibit using a subset of recordings, with selection criteria documented.
Written source B, participant letter: Some contributors welcome an exhibit but worry that a selection of familiar sounds could imply that everyone shares the same experience of a place. They propose including contrasting explanations of a sound where contributors have permitted this. Permission to store a recording is not necessarily permission to play it publicly. The letter asks the group to distinguish absence from the exhibit from absence in the neighbourhood. It does not request that all recordings be played.

Interviewer: The indexing report sounds like a completion milestone. Does it mean the archive is ready for a public exhibit?

Coordinator: It means we can locate and describe everything we received. It doesn't establish that the material represents the whole neighbourhood, or that every recording may be made public. Some contributors agreed to deposit a file for research but asked to be consulted about public playback. The agreement attached to each file has to be checked individually.

Interviewer: Would a selection of contrasting explanations make the exhibit more representative?

Coordinator: It could make the interpretation less one-dimensional. I would resist calling that representativeness, though. We would be selecting contrasting accounts because they illuminate a question, not drawing a sample from a known population. A single sound can have different associations without either account being a mistake.

Interviewer: What would you recommend now?

Coordinator: Prepare a small selection plan that records why each item is proposed, checks permissions and invites feedback on the interpretation. If a recording cannot be cleared, it stays out of the public exhibit. We could use a short written description only if that use is independently permitted. The steering group has not approved an exhibit, and I would not ask it to approve a claim of comprehensive coverage. I would ask it to consider a bounded proposal that can be amended when contributors raise concerns.

- Reasoning / annotation: Seven is the start time, thread is the participant's responsibility, fabric is supplied. Three euros is a charge, not a time.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: Listen for verbs such as bring, supply and cost; do not put every mentioned object into the bring list.

blocks.title: LIS-B1-01 — Choosing a reliable journey
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Distinguish a speaker's concession from the overall judgment and its condition.
- Independent worked example: Example text: The digital menu is convenient for many visitors, although some prefer a printed menu. The café should offer both formats when possible.
- Reasoning / annotation: Although acknowledges a limitation; the final recommendation is conditional. It is not a rejection of the digital menu.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: Replay around the contrast and conclusion; retain qualifiers instead of converting them to always or never.

blocks.title: SPE-A2-01 — Talk about your routine
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Situation: describe a favourite weekend outing. Idea bank: place, one action, one feeling, one reason. Toolkit: On Saturdays…; then…; I enjoy… because…
- Independent worked example: Independent model: On Sundays, I visit the market with my uncle. Then we look at the flower stalls. I enjoy going there because the flowers are beautiful. We usually head home after that.
- Reasoning / annotation: Annotation: the time phrase establishes the situation; then connects actions; because explains a preference. Avoid a list of disconnected nouns.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: New practice: describe an afternoon at a community festival. Plan three keywords (place/action/reason), put the model away, speak for 20–40 seconds, and check whether the sequence and reason were clear. No required recording, grade or oral proficiency evidence.

blocks.title: SPE-B1-01 — Explain and support an opinion
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Situation: explain a preference about a public space. Idea bank: purpose, benefits, trade-off, example. Toolkit: I'd prefer…; One reason is…; For instance…; On the other hand…
- Independent worked example: Independent model: I'd prefer more trees in the square. They provide shade, which makes the space comfortable. For instance, someone waiting for a friend could sit out of the sun. An open area might be better for a large event.
- Reasoning / annotation: Annotation: a concrete example supports the reason; the alternative is acknowledged without withdrawing the original preference. Avoid repeating the claim as its own reason.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: New practice: should a community hall have a mural or a display of local history? Plan position/reason/example/alternative in keywords; close the model, speak aloud, then answer when the other choice might be useful. Self-check coherence and fair qualification. No required recording, score or oral proficiency evidence.

blocks.title: LIS-A1-01 — A school club announcement
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Find the event first; on a replay listen for one detail at a time.
- Independent worked example: Example text (not audio): The dance show is in Hall C on Sunday. It begins at half past six.
- Reasoning / annotation: The event is a dance show. Hall C is where, and half past six is when. Do not write a place in the time box.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: If you miss a detail, listen again for the relevant place or time word.

blocks.title: LIS-A2-02 — A changed plan for Saturday
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Track the earlier plan, the revision and its reason in separate columns.
- Independent worked example: Example text: We planned to rehearse outside, but the ground is wet, so we'll practise in the gym instead. The rehearsal lasts an hour.
- Reasoning / annotation: Outside was the earlier plan. The wet ground explains the change; the gym is the updated place. The duration is separate.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: On replay, listen around but, so and instead; do not keep the old arrangement as the new one.

blocks.title: LIS-B1-02 — Discussing a group-project problem
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Map the obstacle, suggested response and constraint; check the agreed action.
- Independent worked example: Example text: A: The costumes do not fit all performers. B: We can adjust the sleeves, but the fabric is limited. A: Let's alter only the ones that restrict movement. B: Agreed.
- Reasoning / annotation: The fabric constraint explains why they choose a limited alteration rather than altering every costume.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: If several responses are discussed, listen for acceptance and the condition that shapes it.

blocks.title: LIS-A2-03 — Choosing a class at the sports centre
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Compare alternatives against the speaker's actual constraint; infer only from stated information.
- Independent worked example: Example text: A: Shall we order the large desk? B: It won't fit in the alcove. A: The narrow one has fewer drawers. B: That's fine; it will fit.
- Reasoning / annotation: The narrow desk meets the space requirement. More drawers are not decisive because the large desk will not fit.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: Track option, constraint and response; an attractive feature does not prove a final preference.

blocks.title: LIS-B1-04 — Planning a student podcast episode
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Distinguish a preference, a compromise and the condition attached to it.
- Independent worked example: Example text: A: I'd prefer a full menu. B: We have one oven available. A: Then a smaller menu makes sense, provided we can include a vegetarian dish. B: We can do that.
- Reasoning / annotation: A prefers the full menu but accepts a smaller one if the vegetarian dish is included. This is conditional acceptance.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: Do not treat a preference as the final decision; listen for provided, if and the other person's response.

blocks.title: LIS-A1-03 — The Bakery Order
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Keep the first request separate from the final choice.
- Independent worked example: Example text: A: A yellow balloon, please. B: We only have orange ones. A: I'll take an orange one.
- Reasoning / annotation: The yellow balloon was requested, but the last line changes the choice. The final item is orange.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: On replay, follow the words after the change rather than stopping at the first request.

blocks.title: LIS-A1-04 — My New Neighbour
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Attach each detail to the person or thing it describes.
- Independent worked example: Example text: Leo likes chess. His cousin Sam likes singing. They often visit a pond.
- Reasoning / annotation: Chess belongs to Leo; singing belongs to Sam. A nearby name is not always the person described.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: On replay, make one small note per person; do not swap the two.

blocks.title: LIS-A1-05 — The Missing Hat
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Listen for corrections, then match the complete description.
- Independent worked example: Example text: A: Is this your striped bag? B: No, mine has circles. A: Here is a bag with circles. B: Yes, that's mine.
- Reasoning / annotation: The first bag is rejected. Circles identify the bag in the final exchange; stripes do not.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: If two descriptions sound similar, replay the correction before deciding.

blocks.title: LIS-A2-04 — Changing Trains After a Delay
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Distinguish an earlier arrangement from an alternative, and the reason from the action.
- Independent worked example: Example text: The outdoor film screening is unavailable because the projector has failed. We can watch a different film indoors, but we need to collect new passes first.
- Reasoning / annotation: The projector failure explains the change. The indoor film is an alternative; collecting passes is a step before it.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: Replay to link the action to the selected alternative, not to the unavailable plan.

blocks.title: LIS-A2-05 — An Art Exhibition Reminder
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: A reminder can revise one instruction while leaving other information in place.
- Independent worked example: Example text: For the craft demonstration, use the upstairs studio, not the courtyard. Your original reservation is still valid. Please switch off notifications during the talk.
- Reasoning / annotation: The location changes; the reservation does not. The last sentence is a request, not another location.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: Listen for not, still and please; mark change, unchanged condition and instruction separately.

blocks.title: LIS-A2-06 — Repairing a Bicycle
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Distinguish a possibility from a promise, and a suggestion from an accepted plan.
- Independent worked example: Example text: A: The tailor may finish your jacket this evening. B: I need it for a ceremony. A: You could wear the plain coat. B: Yes, I'll do that.
- Reasoning / annotation: May is uncertain, not a promise. The plain coat is first a suggestion, then accepted by the final response.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: Replay the response to each suggestion; do not turn may into will.

blocks.title: LIS-B1-05 — A Library of Things
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Follow how a speaker's position develops; identify the reason for a change rather than guessing a feeling.
- Independent worked example: Example text: A: I'm doubtful about the new noticeboard. B: It will include a large-print section. A: That addresses my main concern. I'd support a trial.
- Reasoning / annotation: The speaker moves from doubt to support for a trial because the concern is addressed. The speaker has not endorsed permanent adoption.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: Compare the initial and final statements; preserve the scope of the final commitment.

blocks.title: LIS-B1-06 — What We Learned from a Pop-Up Sale
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Separate what happened from the speaker's later interpretation and next action.
- Independent worked example: Example text: Our choir's first rehearsal sounded uneven. We changed the seating, and the voices blended better. I realised that the arrangement mattered more than singing louder. Next week, we'll test two layouts.
- Reasoning / annotation: Changing seats is the action; better blending is the observed result. The final insight concerns arrangement, and the next test is still planned.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: Use separate notes for event, result, interpretation and future plan; do not turn the insight into an observed fact.

blocks.title: LIS-B1-07 — Checking a Photo Before Sharing
blocks.approved_block:
- Strategy / situation: Separate direct observations, possible interpretations and evidence limits.
- Independent worked example: Example text: A: The attendance register shows fewer visitors this month. B: Perhaps the new timetable matters, but we haven't asked them. A: We should collect responses before changing the schedule.
- Reasoning / annotation: Fewer visits is an observation; the timetable is a possible explanation, not established causation. Responses are proposed as additional evidence.
- Pitfall repair / independent practice: If a claim sounds confident, check whether the speaker actually provides support; preserve perhaps and other limits.
